LOCAL（国内）
NEWS
9/19~9/21 KANAZAWA JAZZ STREET 2026／
金沢ジャズストリート2026
2026年9月6日
岡崎凛

本年のKANAZAWA JAZZ STREET（金沢ジャズストリート）は、2026年９月１９日（土）～２１日（月・祝）の３日間開催される。また９月１８日（金）には前夜祭レセプションライブが予定されている。

2009年にスタートし、今年で１７回目を迎えるKANAZAWA JAZZ STREETは、金沢市中心部の観光名所、ホール、広場など、街のあちこちがライブ会場となる音楽イベントであり、例年多くの音楽ファンが集う。昨年度は総勢１５０を超える団体が出演。今年も国内外からの招聘アーティストをフィーチャーした有料コンサートに加えて、観覧無料のステージが多数企画されている。
神社の境内や美術館などが会場となり、参加者が金沢市の歴史と文化に触れる機会が生れることだろう。「能登復興支援特別ステージ（入場無料）」では、能登半島地震からの復興支援を呼びかける。KANAZAWA JAZZ STREETは、最近海外アーティストの招聘にも積極的であり、企画からは国際的な音楽交流の場を築こうとする思いが感じられる。

items.body: The big guns are absent from post-rock this fall, leaving plenty of space for the next generation to move in. The last article in our Fall Music Preview includes American Primitive, chamber rock, post-metal and prog, with a little bit of folk and jazz thrown in for good measure. Already we’ve covered hundreds of releases, far too many to fit in our daily review section. As fall is the biggest release season for music, we expect the rapid pace of announcements to continue over the next few months. Be sure to visit our Upcoming Releases page as more titles are added daily! Our cover image comes from Kukangendai‘s Baquet Wheel, covered below. Philadelphia’s Hour continues to be the spiritual successor to Rachel’s. Blending chamber arrangements with a post-rock sensibility, the ever-morphing ensemble straddles genres and exudes a sense of elegance. Ghost Bridge is Hour’s first studio album since 2024’s Ease the Work, and contains moments both intimate and immense (Dear Life, October 9). Stepping out from his Blue Lake moniker, Jason Dungen teams up with Johan Carøe for Routine, which operates as a tribute to domestic life. The album feels like family and home, refuge and safety (Tonal Union, September 25).   We might call HUG a supergroup, as it is comprised of Devendra Banhart, Gyan Riley and Noah Georgeson. The guitar work is intricate and instinctive, and in lead single “Cow With Half Moon Passed,” one can even hear the evening frogs singing along (Luaka Bop, September 11). Twenty years into their career, Kyoto’s Kukangendai is still going strong. Recorded live, Baquet Wheel is an acoustic adventure rife with experimentation and a sense of fun (Marionette, October 4). Bass flute and Moog is a rare combination, owned by Big Bend + a&h on their new album Cloudshaped. The title is fitting, as these amorphous pieces twist and turn, dissolve and reform. Piano, strings, sax, bowed psaltery and more play supporting roles (Dead Currencies, September 25).   While Light Conductor‘s music is often described as “cosmic drone,” we feel it fits more in the categories of rock and folk. This is not to say that the former tag is a misnomer, as both elements are present. Sequence Three is the concluding chapter of a triptych, and is one of three records being released by Constellation on September 25. Oren Ambarchi‘s Cooked isn’t just about the guitar; shō, gamelan and a host of other instruments come into play, thanks to a host of guest stars. With one track per side, the compositions have a copious amount of room (Drag City, September 25). Bhajan Bhoy returns with Electrisol, a shimmering guitar set preceded by the single Palidena, which was originally included on a benefit compilation (Feeding Tube/Cardinal Fuzz). RYMDEN looks an awful lot like Kraftwerk on the Bandcamp page for Today May Be Tomorrow. Their sound incorporates jazz, groove, prog and krautrock, lively and loose (Jazzland recordings Norway, September 25). Midway between Acoustic Ladyland and Melt Yourself Down is Pete Wareham’s lost album with Silver Birch, a blast of punk energy, rhythmic improv and fresh saxophone air. After 15 years, High on the Western Hill still sounds new (Kit, November 13).   Lummernikt is an intricate acoustic guitar album, named after the spores of plants once used for theatrical pyrotechnics. The title might also be applied to the music, which flows like a summer river until it reaches the rapids. Finn Loxbo‘s track titles also have intriguing explanations, with references to poetry, prose, nature and children’s toys (Fönstret, September 18). Half of Mountains returns with Nightlife, demonstrating a surprising jazz bent rather than the expected drone. Koen Holtkamp introduces the set with the hypnotic video for “Slow Fox Run.”(Western Vinyl, October 9). We normally find Hausu Mountain in our Electronic section, but Crying Laughing‘s Talking is a different animal: a jazz and funk-laden excursion with healthy doses of percussion (including cowbell!), alto sax and “Ricemeat” (September 10). Eiderdown Records started the season early, releasing two new albums yesterday. Nick Jonah Davis‘ Rose Delta Rising lies on the border of post-rock, gentle and kind, but with upbeat numbers like “Poa Kichizi” to get the crowds dancing. Steven R. Smith‘s Half Light Unfolding operates in a similar tonal range, with guitar, piano and organ, an intimate set that calms the heart and warms the spirit. For a discount, purchase as a pair!   Allison De Groot‘s clawhammer banjo meets Rich Ruth‘s diverse instrumentation on their self-titled LP, whose tones range from lullaby to campfire stomp, with electronic surprises in-between. “10-14” is our favorite (Western Vinyl, October 2). Davide Cedolin follows his Ligurian Pastoral series with Cjera Aʃìn, which is informed by the artist’s “origin land” of Val d’Arzino in Northern Italy. Graced by field recordings from the region, the album is a mix of American primitive, folk and drone, and has a homespun, deep woods tone, perfect for its release on the precipice of the autumnal equinox (September 21). Debacle Records is the new home for Verdin Brothers, who combine field recordings, bluegrass and hauntology on The Crooked Serpent, a collection of late night tales told by a crackling fire (October 16).   What’s on your Dance Card? Adam Hill‘s album includes modern composition and pedal steel!). With seven different composers and a decet, the surprises keep coming, while the fascination level remains high (September 18). The Mexican guitar duo Rodrigo y Gabriela makes a joyful noise with pieces inspired by “rogue monsters, celestial birds and other fantastical creatures.” On one track they become a trio, but OurHome sounds like the work of a quartet (ATO, September 18). Hannes Kretzer‘s music lurks before it pounces, catching listeners off guard like helpless prey. The intensely cinematic Amor Fati sounds like the work of a full band, especially at the rocking end of tracks such as “Devotion & Decay.” Recorded in a 16th century castle church, the album includes guest vocals from Vargkvint and may inspire listeners to develop their own narratives (September 25). Shipwreck Orchestra is not actually an orchestra, but it may as well be, since frontman Aaron Miller plays over a dozen instruments, enhanced by the contributions of a small number of friends. On Papers Relating to an Unattributed Journal, participants use 19th century instruments to weave a conceptual tale (September 11). From the title and artist name, we knew that Glorious 70mm‘s Death Is for Mortals No Longer an Evil, But a Blessing was a pure post-rock album. What we couldn’t tell was that it was a solo effort: immense in sound, difficult to bring on tour. The sound seems tailor-made for silent film scoring, reflecting the wise moniker (September 4). On the same day, Northampton post-rock quartet AV Sunset releases Vs Reality, whose sequences of sweetness are balanced by cathartic explosions, demonstrated in the center of “The Cheerleading Elite” (September 4).   The sound of Edmonton’s Pigeon Breeders lies somewhere between post-rock and noise rock; Springtime as Violence, justifies its title with subtle distortion and thick surges of sound (Honey Farm, September 4). Collapse Under the Empire’s Chris Burda steps out on his own as Age of Life, unveiling the ambitious, cinematic Emergence – Part I. Each track corresponds to a unique era of evolutionary time (CB, October 30). Swiss post-prog rockers hubris. are already on their fifth album, preceded by the Tolkien-inspired single “Death.” White Shores is out September 10. Want even heavier stuff? Try Ølyp, whose energetic progressive metal is enhanced by viola, violin and cello, the sugar to their salt. I(m)MORAL is available on sunshine splatter vinyl and preceded by the head-banging The Human Error (Klonosphere, September 25). Ovoo (not to be confused with OvO) unleashes Obsidian on October 2, with blasts of guitar fury so powerful they blow the top off the mountain, as seen on the cover. Spoken word passages only add to the drama. We hope that you’ve enjoyed our Fall Music Preview and that we’ve given you plenty to look forward to! Richard Allen

items.body: LEENALCHI restage a moment from Korean court speech in “Crying Softshell Turtle.” 별주부가 울며 여짜오되 is the narrator’s cue, spoken in the deeply honorific register a subject uses addressing a king: “Officer Turtle, weeping, humbly says to the king.” It repeats three times across the lyrics, each time introducing a new plea from a soldier turtle on his knees before the Dragon King, begging to cut open a captured rabbit’s belly before the animal talks its way out of the trap. LEENALCHI is a seven-piece band from Seoul, four pansori-trained singers fronting two bassists and a drummer. Park Soo Bum, Choi Su In, Ra Seo Jin and Ahn Yi Ho carry the story’s different voices and its narration between them, while bassists Jang Young Gyu and Ejae lock into drummer Oh Hyung Suk‘s groove underneath. That groove tightens hard on the KCRW session. Midway through the track, the two basses drive into a punk-edged instrumental break that sharpens the standoff between the turtle’s frantic pleading and the rabbit’s swagger, and the singers trade lines rather than harmonise over it, snapping into pansori’s guttural, high-pitched delivery to voice each character as the scene turns. The rabbit gets the last word, daring them to open him up: “You will find nothing but dung.” The song comes from Sugungga, an 18th-century pansori epic about a Dragon King who can only be cured by a rabbit’s liver and the turtle sent to fetch it, and LEENALCHI built their 2020 album of the same name by stripping that centuries-old sung narration down to bass, drums and voice. Bassist Jang Young Gyu leads the band and has also scored the films The Wailing and Train to Busan, and this year has been a busy one under his watch: LEENALCHI signed to Luaka Bop, released the EP Here Comes That Crow in June, and will finally put Sugungga out worldwide on 2 October. The release opens a fall tour that runs through the US before crossing into Europe in mid-November, with UK dates in Dublin, London, Bristol, Leeds and Manchester closing out the run. items.body: Review by tszirmay — By now, It must be suitable for me to tip my cap to the Malcolm/Mark pairing, a London project that has kept a prolific and qualitative progression ( that confounded word, again!) and I have been following closely since I purchased the "Nostalgia for Infinity" (2020) album. Their recent output consists of three out and out jewels, which have been critically acclaimed, and there is no reason to doubt that this new 2026 effort would not make anyone lose their hair to baldness. With Parallel Lives, the dynamic duo throw no curves that may sidetrack their strengths, focusing on the premise that the shortest distance between two points may perhaps be a straight line, but why not offer 11 tracks (2 extras being radio edits), all neatly equivalent? "My Blistering Mind" could easily be referring to the blistering Gartland bass line that decorates this brainy track that seems to cause havoc with the splinters stuck in their collective cortex , both sides being roughed up with a punky tinge that has always been present in the HOGIA stylistic. Its not only a catchy opener but its obsessive quality is quantified by the backing vocal effort that really sets this track apart from the mundane. Coming as a wonderful surprise, "The Mandatory Prize" (rogue poetry in lotion!) keeps their quirky musical gift firmly tongue in cheek, a brooding critique of societal hypocrisy, which let's face it, is something only humans can indulge in with sadistic pleasure, save a hyena and perhaps also a scorpion (the first killing others for sheer pleasure and the other wilfully murdering themselves). Lose when you win, indeed. The musical tone is correctly pugnacious. Flip that damn switch and out of the wild blue yonder comes a gorgeous and charming instrumental that knocked me sideways, "Never Really Felt Like Home" conveys a sense of lukewarm regret, far from anger but surely in bed with despondence. Guest Kathryn Thomas uses a variety of flutes to underscore one of the finest melodies heard in recent years, a superb slice of yearning. Prog rapping comes unwrapped (clever again) on "Smile, Smile, Smile" , a shivering electronic riff skipping over an intense spoken word that starts out accepting and turning into gentlemanly rage. 'Nobody knows who you are', even yourself I guess and frankly, what is existence all about ? Accumulating wealth and power? No, the answer is in the title: be happy and smile, repeated three times for effect. Fertig !Jazz it up, will you now! "Intermission" has the Tangent/Andy Tillison vibe that highlights a wide range of classic mood swings (accent on the swing part) , a ruthless bass exercise (both musicians are incredible but I have a well-known fetish for the bass guitar and Gatland ranks as one of my perennial faves), a marvelous interlude that will set-up the suave beauty of the title track, a heart-felt love song that is progged up with delicate detail, and gratefully stripped down to the basics : voice, piano and distant percussion. And tons of fervent emotion, eyes closed, ears open. The chosen melodic line is another example of their attention to feeling ,a masterful stroke of genius. Waking up from the dream, prompted from a remote command , the somewhat more energetic "Eversion" revives the fiery anger this band manages on an even par with their melancholy, a slightly deranged and obsessive look into the mirror of past lives still unsettled. Essentially a vortex of circular sonic turbulence, the voice and that darn bass confusing the issues with a wide variety of counterstrokes and pushback. Malcolm finally whips out his electric guitar and goes on zippered tear, a short slash that only reinvigorates the urge to hold on and seek help. Seven minutes of intensity. Opting for an compulsive electronic diversion (which they use regularly but only with surgical precision) "Pretty Blue Fox" is another thrilling instrumental that certainly invokes images of parallel realms, a dreamscape of unusual consequence and open to individual conjecture. The keyboard work is exemplary (the piano in particular) and adapted to the overall tendency of this recording. Well played! Back to in-your-face simplicity on the ear-friendly "Just Another Thing", Malcolm speeding through the lyrics like an F1 McLaren race car, vroom-vroom pursuit, 'to add to the list', a checkered flag synthesizer flutter to keep the engines oiled, the bass pistons throttling loudly, and the rubber smoking. Punk-prog. Attached is the outro instrumental "Dropping the Mask", proving once and for evermore that the main attraction of this act is their aptitude to balance worded and non-worded material without losing any talent or identity . If the glove fits?The epic two-part finale "Just Hold On" is a glowing tribute to the hyperactive societal burden we must all bear, where time and space are blurred into an algo rhythmic smear that keeps us from restful peace of mind or quiet critical thinking. The opening choir section underlines that agony, the electric guitar somehow hopeful, the bass thoughtfully gentle, eventually building up the urgency that makes blood circulate in our veins, oxygenizing our brain as well as limbering up our machine's muscles. Malcolm vocal is more of a sermon to the times, the lyrics depressive and apathetic but the message combative and resilient. Its never too late. Happiness and contentment can be a as simple as a forceful decision, a basic choice, to just HOLD ON. Take my hand and get this album, it just might help the healing process we humans all deserve. Its not too late. The shortened radio edits of the first two tracks are oddly enough not edits as they are the same length or even longer than the originals, Brits have the best sense of humor, sardonic and off the wall. Their absolute finest effort by a country mile. Hats off !5 corresponding existences

items.body: Review by OlyaBeginner — I am not an expert in music, so I cannot always explain exactly what musical techniques create these feelings. 1. Jungle WaltzAn interesting combination of vocals and musical instruments immediately catches attention. There is a bright transition into a denser part, which is then replaced by another mood, more positive and mysterious. The sound feels quite exotic, with a gradual addition of more intensity. As the composition develops, it becomes more epic and mysterious. It feels like entering an unknown world and slowly discovering what is inside it. 2. Meekness and GentlenessVery cheerful, pleasant, and light-hearted. I had an association with the beauty of fast movement. The composition creates a very joyful mood and seems to encourage the listener to move and enjoy life. Despite its somewhat gloomy beginning, it becomes very alive and energetic. It leaves a feeling of happiness and lightness.3. Lavoro d'AmoreThe beginning feels very friendly and welcoming, creating a warm and pleasant mood. Gradually, it changes into a deeper and more noble feeling of love, which seems to fill the whole soul and elevate it to another level. It feels like love requires some difficult work and effort, but after this work is done, peace and harmony finally arrive.4. Be Ye Not UnwiseThe beginning is very gloomy and perhaps reflects the consequences of unwise human behaviour. The listener is surrounded by a very dark and almost hopeless atmosphere. There is a strong feeling of sadness and sorrow, which seems to reflect the horror of human recklessness. At some point, the music creates a feeling of emptiness, as if nothing can be changed anymore.5. Passing OverThe composition has a touching and cozy beginning, which gradually develops into a brighter but still very emotional atmosphere. Then there is a sudden transition back to a more tender feeling. After that, the emotions become much stronger, and the atmosphere grows more intense. It inspires the listener to struggle, work hard, and keep moving forward.Eventually, the tension decreases and the music becomes more peaceful and measured. It feels like a transition from struggle to acceptance and harmony, both with the surrounding world and with oneself.6. PremonitionThe beginning feels like the birth of a certain feeling. The listener seems to be paying attention to very small and almost unnoticeable details. Gradually, this feeling becomes stronger and starts to influence the person. It feels as if someone trusts their intuition, and this gives them a direction for moving forward.Later, the music becomes more brutal and perhaps more confident, almost as if the person becomes sure that they are right. Finally, everything becomes calmer, creating a feeling of satisfaction because the intuition turned out to be correct. The whole composition feels very epic and touching.7. Patience of HopeHope is a very important part of life, especially in our time. The composition begins in a touching way and then moves into a faster tempo, creating an atmosphere of movement and life. It slows down and then accelerates again, which gives the listener energy and inspires them to work and live despite difficulties.Later, the music seems to reach a higher level of immersion. It can be connected with faith that everything will eventually be fine. I like the combination of inspiration and calmness here. It gives strength without creating too much tension. 8. Her LoveA very sweet and energetic beginning reflects strength and hard work. Then the music becomes lighter and more energetic. There is a feeling of sincerity and care, which later can become lost in the difficulties and struggles that appear in relationships.At the same time, there is passion and strong involvement, which can also create complications. However, persistence and the desire to preserve the relationship make it possible to overcome these difficulties. The composition feels like a story about love that is not always easy but is worth making an effort for.9. Through Difficult DecisionsA feeling of warmth and joy fills the soul here, although it does not come without effort. This makes the experience of life more interesting and meaningful. The composition creates a very full and uplifting atmosphere.Perhaps it is also about one's worldview. If a person loves life and remains true to themselves, even difficult decisions may become less difficult to make. There is a feeling that being honest with yourself gives you the strength to move through complicated situations.10. Psalm 6The fast tempo at the beginning seems to represent difficult trials and heavy experiences. Then comes a moment of despair, sadness, and anxiety. However, it feels as if the person realizes that they cannot remain in this state forever and starts searching for hope.This journey is not easy. It requires courage and determination to escape from despair. The composition creates an atmosphere of inner struggle, where courage and strength of spirit are necessary to continue moving forward.I really enjoyed listening to this album. It is the kind of music that ennobles the soul.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Kansas. Toto, Len Dawson, Patrick Mahones and the band that put the Mid-West state on the prog billboards worldwide, wayward sons like dust in the wind. Here is Quivira , Jake Livgren on vocals (does the name ring a bell?), the thrilling Lisa Larue on keyboards, her recent Rematrination debut left me in awe. Filling out the trio is guitarist John Baker who has worked with Mars Hollow and Forever Twelve. Within a mere 6 seconds of the intro, "The Coming of the Spaniards", my experienced ears immediately sent the following message to my brain, 'this is going to be very very good'. Its all there: massive choirs echoing cross the sandy valleys, concentrated symphonics with a colossal Iberian influence on the acoustic guitar, interweaving conquering violins, elegance in the piano structure and loads of cinematic grandeur. Yes, I am still exhaling ?.On that note, "The Benefits of Breathing Quietly" has Joe Denizon's crafty violin leading the way, passing the baton to Jake's expansive voice, a commanding pulmonary delivery where both tone and delivery hold hands in interlocked splendour, and Lisa's synths flirt unashamedly with the catskin gasps. She also dazzles on the piano as well taking care of the programmed drums (which are expertly designed.A cunning play on words with "The Plain's Truth", equally clever musically, as the fluttering violin plays the lead to perfection, building up the fury courtesy of John's superlative note bending (both the 6 and 4 string varieties), a merging of sounds totally in harmony with one another, eventually painting the vast landscape of both arid mesas and endless grasslands beyond. The acoustic guitar cannot help to revive that Hispanic sentiment, a dramatic sonic statement of intent. Time to dive into more classic prog-rock initiatives, surely evoking the legendary Kansas overtly melodic bombast, Lisa Larue in particular shining brightly on her various keys, she is truly a star to reckon with. More passionate violin to remind us that its all about feeling, touch and caress. "Quivira Bound" becomes all fussed up with a twangy guitar solo that sparkles in the rain, the e-piano lull a momentary reflection of light, before Jake goes for another round on the microphone. Damn impressive. Wide screen smoothness on the ripping "Moving Forward", shifting gears into a musical cruise control, letting the electric guitar, violin and synths solo to their hearts content. Baker's raunchy axe will surely blow a few tumble weeds into the mix, a stunning spotlight that nails the tombstone coffin tight. The violin setting features a two-track splurge that is equally mind blowing. The programmed drums are stupendously effective here, some prog purists hate the idea as a rule but frankly, the technology has certainly evolved from the old TR-808, as the title may imply. This is a headline piece of musical genius. Everything changes on "The Turk/Follow the Wind", namely the mood, the sound and the vocal style, a shocking variation that gives more pavement to the highway ahead. The sultry violin commands the instrumental cavalry once again, leading the charge as the storytelling suggests a look back at times gone by, when nature held firm against the conquest of the wild, wild west . We now reach the heart of the sunrise, so to speak, with two of the longer tracks (both 7?8-minute range) that will define the core of the album, especially in a progressive context, as they are intricate workouts that ooze endeavour, aptitude and mature vision. "Nothing is Everything" is a fast-paced symphonic extravaganza that hesitates not one iota in getting into the nitty-gritty. Lisa's solo piano sections are to die for, the inserting violin sizzle adding to the fire, the arrangement expanding into a gargantuan crescendo that keeps accelerating into a near frenzy. Its so explosive and stimulating, and as the final segment reveals a gentler outcome, one realizes that the question has been answered. Nothing is everything. Spectacular. "Carved from the Sun" reveals a more groove orientation, almost like a driving down the freeway in a convertible, the throttling bass mercilessly crushing the gravel, the brassy guitar spiralling in full control, kicking up a vast wall of smoke that can be seen for miles and miles. The spirit is warm yet airy, bright and surely windy. This is 'close your eyes and imagine' style of prog that should impress even the most finnicky prog fans out there, equally grandiose and mesmerizing, and deeply committed to pleasure. I mean, wow!"Kicking Rocks" (a great way to damage your toes out in the mountains) expresses perfectly the foundation of this muscular piece, not at all 'hard or heavy' but certainly beefy and athletic. Lisa's piano proves her immense versatility, her fingers creating evocative images of strength and movement. When John decides that he needs to 'ramble on', he does so with gusto, bravado and tornado, flicking big swaths of thrills. Expertly planned album as this clearly is, the final two tracks seek to reestablish a connection with the opening tracks, the violin /piano interaction returning to the front of the stage on "Prelude to Anywhere /Weekend Conquistadors", a recurring vocal presentation where the epic story nears its natural conclusion. The upsurge is obvious, the mood settles and some brief narration expounds the message. I am 'Still Breathing", though barely, as the emotions I have felt listening to this work has overcome my sense of critical thinking, a somewhat similar effect as falling in love (where reason kneels before the heart), and the realization that this final and momentous piece encapsulates the entire hour and 6 minutes spent in its glorified presence. Surely, among the top candidates for album of the year but unchallengeable winner of debut of the year! The horse has run away?..5 Flight of eagles

items.body: Composer Anthony Davis Anthony Davis has never hesitated to share express his feelings and politics in his music. His operas “X: The Life and Times of Malcolm X” (1986) and “Amistad” (1997) are two recent shining examples. Album Cover This most recent of his operas is also one that partakes of more recent political events than the previously mentioned works. It is, by my count, his 8th opera. And though all of Davis’ operas can be said to have some political content, “X”, “Amistad”, and now “The Central Park Five (2019), are most specifically focused on the transatlantic slave trade (ca. 1500- 1870) and subsequent black political history.. Librettist Richard Wesley The story captured in the libretto by Richard Wesley made newspaper headlines and even motivated the pre presidential Donald Trump to take out full page ad in several media publications advocating their guilt and advocating for the death penalty. Performance photo by JJ Geiger While I have had the pleasure of multiple hearings of this powerful and substantial work I have chosen to include the composer’s excellent essay which describes not only the story but also the some of the intricacies and references embedded in the music itself. Notes on The Central Park Five By Anthony Davis 1989. A group of predominantly Black and Hispanic teenagers enter Central Park in New York City. They turnover garbage cans, throw rocks, harass people on bicycles. A young woman is sexually assaulted in the Park and six teenagers are detained and questioned about the assault. Five of the teenagers, Kevin Richardson, Raymond Santana, Korey Wise, Yusef Salaam and Antron McCray become the center of a criminal case that would polarize New York City. The Exonerated Five were falsely accused and convicted of the crime with no physical evidence. Condemned publicly by the press, the Exonerated Five were victims in a culture war waged against  Black and Hispanic communities.  A politically ambitious real estate mogul condemns the teenagers with a full page add, proclaiming “Bring Back the Death Penalty. Bring Back Our Police!” The persecution of the Central Park Five marks the beginning of Donald Trump’s political career, built on racial animus and the exploitation of the deep rooted racial divide in America.  Why? What accounts for what Johnny Cochran would later famously call, “The rush to judgement.” How could the court trust the coerced “confessions” of the five teenagers? How did we come to this moment that assumed guilt, blindly seeking revenge? What caused the deeply rooted anxiety of White Americans when confronted with Black-Hispanic culture  and people?  1989. Spike Lee’s movie Do the Right Thing premieres, Quincy Jones’ album “Back on the Block” debuts, Black and Hispanic teenagers sing the Tone Loc song “Wild Thing” as they descend on the Park. The song becomes a label in the press as they describe the actions in the Park as “Wilding in the Park.” Did the persecution of the Five represent the White anxiety about Hip Hop entering mainstream American culture? Was the response to the Five a reflection of Tony in the Pizza restaurant smashing Radio Raheem’s boombox? The persecution of the Central Park Five, emblematic of other similar incidents of false accusations of Black and Hispanic men  across the country, demonstrates the devastating consequence of the culture war, as incarceration has become the new slavery. As a composer, I have always been drawn to stories that intersect the political and cultural worlds. My operas, X: The Life and Times of Malcolm X, Amistad, Wakonda’s Dream, Tania and Pancho Rabbit and the Coyote, all explore political moments and movements that are reflected in the dynamic of music. In X, it is the evolution of creative music from the forties to the sixties, a revolutionary movement in music as well as in politics. In Amistad, it is the false balance of the Missouri Compromise and the untenable grounding of America’s birth in both the ideals of Democracy and the original sin of Slavery. In American music one must always understand the irony that slavery created our culture from the advent of the minstrel show to the “Birth of the Cool.” Music can capture the tensions and fissures in our cultural and political life and the hope of something better. Music can allow us to feel the powerful forces at play in our lives, forces that are at once destructive but yet in our cathartic engagement allow us to envision a kind of freedom. The Prologue of The Central Park Five begins with the “Exonerated Five” today as they reflect on the past. The opening cross-fade with the Kurzweil texture signify a fissure, a break, the dark spectre of trauma. Each of the Five recalls the trauma of the past. Librettist Richard Wesley ends the Prologue with poignant simplicity, “They tell us in school how big the world is, but that’s their world. They crushed mine.” Act One introduces a recurring theme and harmony that suggests the past world of Harlem. The lyric, “Harlem, a Black and Tan Fantasy,” of course, suggests Ellington’s Harlem. In fact, before the Masque’s aria, the descending minor 3rd in the baritone saxophone suggests Ellington’s famous Tone Parallel to Harlem from 1949. Ellington describes the descending 3rds that appear throughout the work as signifying and enunciating “Harlem.” The theme is introduced by the Baritone Saxophone and starts as a dirge with variations. The harmony in f minor recalls one of Charles Mingus’ most famous harmonic progressions loosely based on the standard, “You Don’t Know What Love Is,” a ballad made famous by Billie Holiday. The melody is then played by the trombone with a counter-melody inspired by the great Eric Dolphy, played by the Baritone Saxophone and the Bass Clarinet. The theme moves into swing with an iteration by the trumpet. This introduces the Masque’s aria, “Harlem, a Black and Tan Fantasy.” The Masque is a malevolent force in the opera. He is the skeptical reporter, who distrusts Black people. He’s the policeman who arrests and interrogates the five suspects. He is the judge who condemns them. In Act One the five singers become their younger selves, before they arrive in Central Park. They are exuberant and recklessly free as they talk about their lives and aspirations. The music begins in a gamelan inspired texture with a 9 beat pattern in the vibraphone  and right hand of the piano and a 10 beat pattern in the left hand of the piano. This creates a repeating grid of 90 beats. As in my first opera, X, often I try to marry underlying rhythmic structures with dramatic intent. Every 90 beats something new can happen in the music and in the drama. The orchestra slowly reveals the inner harmonic working of the drone against the free flowing lines of the Five boys. The Masque disturbs and interrupts the Five’s music signaled by a series of cascading major thirds that play against the harmony of the drone establishing a 4 against 3 rhythmic tension, as the music evolves “off the grid.” This leads to a new tempo before the Masque proclaims  “They (Black people) are lost!” The opera explores rhythmic tension that is reinforced by the harmony. The Five defiantly sing “This is my world!” and later the anthem “The World is Ours!” The stable harmony of the anthem is eventually disturbed by the building polyrhythms as the Five become more excited culminating in the antiphonal rhythmic interplay between “This is no life. This ain’t living. This ain’t no life!” and “Time to bust out, time to break out, time break out, time to act out” This leads the Five into the Park. In the music, I tried to capture the exhilaration and exuberance of the Five and their illusion of freedom. As they enter the Park, the Five sing, “We are the freaks! We are the freaks who own the night!” The music in the Park is influenced by everything from Parliament Funkadelic to fusion Miles Davis and Jaco Pastorius with Weather Report. The music captures the exuberance and recklessness of the Park that quickly becomes out of control fueled by  groove and funk. Music allows us to see different worlds and to shift perspective. As Kevin and Antron are initially detained we hear the echoes of the Blues and again the stop-time from Black and Tan Fantasy as the Masque declares falsely that “That is the end of that.” The anthem music, when it returns as the Assistant District Attorney and the Masque discuss the assault, becomes a distant, shattered memory. The interrogation scenes feature rhythmically driven music as if an ex-machina force is coercing the Five’s confessions. The words of the Masque and the Assistant D.A. are like weapons. The vocal writing is more angular with shifting harmonic centers emphasizing speech rhythms and repetition as the Masque and A.D.A, try to force the Five to implicate each other. This is in contrast with more reflective moments that are lyrical and harmonically grounded. The Five’s collective sense of apprehension and fear is expressed in passages drawn from the vocal ensemble tradition of close harmony from doo-wop, Motown and the street as if through a filter of Gil Evans’ arrangements in “My Ship” or Blues for Pablo. The hybridity of the music tells the story. A friend once asked me, “How do you write for Donald Trump?” I replied, “First, he is a tenor. Second, he repeats himself in his violent sound bytes. Third, he never completes a sentence.” I tried to capture his use of short, repeating phrases that could be amplified by the chorus. “Wilding, Rampaging, Wilding, Rampaging Wolfpack!” What is Trump’s appeal? Like moths to flame, Trump says things that people may think and be afraid to express. In MAGA world Trump’s racism is somehow authentic and Trump has helped unleash the pathological racism that is both systemic and psychological.  I entertained these scary thoughts as I composed the opera. Finally, the opera is an uplifting story of a community rising up against injustice, of the Five finally finding exoneration and vindication as the anthem returns with “The World is Ours!” But we know the cost, as Korey says, “They stole from me!” And we know this is a continuing story. The forces that implicated the Five are still with us. Thank you to the librettist Richard Wesley who illuminated their story with humanity and emotion from Sheronne Salaam’s “They are trying to blame my son” to Korey’s “They stole from me.” None of this would happen without the love and support of my muse, Cynthia Aaronson-Davisuch passionate command. I must recognize the extraordinary work of Earl Howard who created the electro-acoustic world that shadows the opera. I need to call attention to the critical work of Andreas Mitisek who directed the first production in Long Beach and helped realize the dramatic possibilities of the opera. I am indebted to all the musicians and singers who brought this opera to life in Long Beach, Portland and Detroit and, of course, Long Beach Opera, particularly Jenny Rivera and Michelle Magaldi, who believed in the work and help produce this recording. I would also like to thank UCSD for its continued support of my work. None of this would happen without the love and support of my muse, Cynthia Aaronson-Davis. Another performance photo by JJ Geiger The opera has received many performances since its premiere by The Long Beach Opera, who commissioned the work. It has since been performed in Detroit, New York, and is scheduled for another performance in Long Beach. The music incorporates bebop and other jazz styles into a listener friendly melodic and harmonic constructions that set the beautiful libretto’s words effectively. Davis himself identifies as a politically expressive composer. Even in his non-stage works like his meditation on the first of the so called Miranda Rights (You have the right to remain silent) cast in the classical form of a concerto for clarinet (2007). Arguably, Davis’ work cannot be separated from the experience of Black American culture. Davis, raised in the cultural lineage of transgressional innovators such as George Lewis and his many colleagues of the AACM (American Association of Creative Musicians), a group that still works to include the cultures and rituals of many African countries into the practice of so called western art music). Davis has been a defining figure in contemporary music since at least the 1970s. And now he is recognized as an exemplar of “American” music by virtue of the recognition of the Pulitzer Prize. As a work of classical protest music, it functions (in Jeremy Eichler’s term) as “times echo”, a use of great art to frame a noxious historical event in a sort of time capsule that preserves memories and feelings of the story that lives again in performance. As such, The Central Park Five stands proudly alongside Hans Werner Henze’s “Essay on Pigs” (1968), Benjamin Britten’s “War Requiem” (1961), and composers as diverse as Dmitri Shostakovich, Luigi Nono, Arnold Schoenberg, Steve Reich, Wynton Marsalis, and Louis Andriessen (to name but a few). But, as is the case with any artistic work of protest, the actual impact remains to be seen. The horrors of racism remain a defining part of western culture, of American culture now cast forever in this deeply felt drama. This is definitely not, in Toni Morrison’s phrase, “…music to entertain the master and soothe his blunted soul.” And in a time of the active attempts to suppress and deny this unsavory history, art can preserve memories both good and bad.. There is a noble beauty in that.

items.body: Kregel is a Belgian band from Limburg that formed in 2016. Looking for a short, punchy name, they settled on Kregel—a word that suggests stubbornness, contrariness, and, above all, a refusal to submit. While they describe themselves as a Rock band, that label feels somewhat too broad, as their influences clearly lean towards Post-Punk and New-Wave. One of Kregel’s defining characteristics is that they sing in their native language, Dutch. Their lyrics are personal yet compelling, tackling serious subjects with a touch of humor and a rich sense of imagery. Influences such as Aroma Di Amore are never far away, and listeners will inevitably notice the connection with this important touchstone of the Belgian underground scene. However, Kregel is certainly no cheap imitation; they have developed a distinctive sound and personality of their own. Kregel is an idiosyncratic trio with a strong DIY ethos, a mindset that has resulted in a remarkable discography comprising seven EPs to date. Simply numbered “#1” through “#7”, each release features four exclusive tracks. Their latest EP, “#7”, released on Wagonmaniac Music, is another triumph and the direct inspiration for this interview with Bart Timmermans, Sven Derwa, and Jeroen De Smet. Kregel: a musical treasure from Belgium that has so far remained largely hidden from the rest of the world… (Picture credits by BV Fotografisch Atelier Paul Delaet / Interview courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: If I’m not mistaken, Kregel was founded 10 years ago and has released around seven EPs to date. You are gradually making a name for yourselves in the Flemish underground scene, but to an international audience, you still remain somewhat like ‘aliens’. How would you best introduce Kregel to a wider international audience through your key achievements, influences, and future prospects? Sven: Kregel has been around for about 10 years now. We are a Rock trio consisting of Bart (also frontman of both Vandal X and Flipo Mancini) on vocals, drum and bass programming, and occasional keyboards, while Jeroen and I play guitar. Jeroen: We have been playing together since 2008. At first, we were a quintet (Feetfetish), with Bart playing bass. After the departure of the last/10th drummer, we became a quartet (‘Salk). In 2016, our singer had had enough, Bart took over on vocals, and Kregel was born in its current form. Bart: The best introduction to Kregel can be found on the streaming services, where our tracks are available. What you hear there is Kregel. Presenting ourselves to an international audience is a little more difficult because our lyrics are written in Dutch, and they are just as much a defining part of a Kregel song as the music itself. We would not call ourselves ‘aliens’: we are three friends who have been meeting in a rehearsal basement more or less every week for about 15 years, working on our songs and getting a lot of happiness out of it. Sven: That does not mean our music is necessarily a celebration of happiness and joy, because we write songs about our personal concerns and social issues, and unfortunately, it is not all sunshine and roses… Bart: Apart from the seven EPs we have released so far, there are not many other achievements that would make a huge impression on an international audience. Two notable exceptions are the two support slots we played for P.I.L. in May this year (Mr. Lydon is, after all, the godfather of us all; so we guess all of your readers know him), which received a lot of positive reactions. Jeroen: We should also mention our two ‘international tours’. In 2023, we were invited by the John Peel Centre for Creative Arts in England to play a concert, and we added a pub show in London to the trip. Last autumn, we were invited by Mekanic Bird, a kindred-spirit band from Saint-Omer in northern France, to spend a weekend there playing two bar shows of the kind we usually do: for a very small, but always enthusiastic audience. Sven: What are Kregel’s plans for the future? We hope to make music together for many more years, release EPs, and regularly be invited to play that music live. We like to let things happen naturally, without too much planning. Q: You do not hide the fact that the Post-Punk of the ’80s and ’90s has had a strong influence on your compositions. What exactly made those years and that musical style so magical, and what elements of it still remain today in Kregel’s sound? Bart: The three of us grew up in the 1980s, and that was when our musical tastes were formed. Although we did not know each other at the time, we were apparently all particularly drawn to (Post-)Punk and New-Wave, and to anything that leaned in that direction. It seems obvious to us that those influences resonate in the sound we produce in 2026, but we cannot pinpoint exactly which elements they are. Sven: In any case, it is not as though we had a very specific idea of the sound we wanted to pursue when Kregel was formed. We never even explicitly discussed it. The only starting points we had when we decided to continue as a trio were that the lyrics would be in Dutch, and that we would use a computer as our rhythm section. The ‘Kregel sound’ — insofar as such a thing can be said to exist, because our sound is evolving too — is therefore not the result of extensive prior discussion, but of playing together. The only criterion we use is that all three of us are happy with a song. Q: Internationally, choosing to sing in your native language, Dutch, can be seen as a challenge, but at the same time it highlights your originality—combined with lyrics that are sometimes humorous yet, in my opinion, still carry a certain depth. That raises the question: why singing in Dutch, what is this depths of the lyrical content and is it an option for you to ever sing in another language? Jeroen: As mentioned, choosing to write in Dutch was a conscious decision from the very beginning. We do not want to write throwaway songs, but at the same time, we do not want to put overly explicit ‘messages’ into our lyrics. We want to make songs about subjects and feelings that matter to us and occupy our minds, without wanting to impose anything on our audience. With Kregel, there is no finger-wagging; rather, we use down-to-earth and original ways of expressing our feelings about certain subjects, wrapped up in compact, almost slogan-like lyrics with a large dose of (dark) humour. Bart: All of that would not work for us in a language other than our mother tongue, even if this can be a barrier to our ‘international career’. Moreover, Dutch is a very evocative language, with lots of double meanings and idiomatic expressions, so it can occasionally make a perceptive listener raise an eyebrow. We briefly considered translating the lyrics when we were invited to England, but precisely because of those double meanings and idioms, we could not arrive at an acceptable result, so we decided against it. Sven: On the other hand, the ‘disadvantage’ of making music in a small language should not be overstated: we regularly play in the French-speaking part of Belgium, and the audience reactions are no different from those of Dutch-speaking audiences. We noticed the same thing in England when we were there: the unifying power of music should not be underestimated. Q: Another characteristic of Kregel is that, so far, you have only released EPs, each containing different, exclusive tracks. You are now at seven in total. Why this choice, and what is your stance on releasing a full-length album? Do albums still make sense in a world where most listeners rely on streaming platforms and curated playlists? Bart: The fact that we release our tracks in groups of four on EPs is actually purely coincidental, as is the case with many things involving Kregel. In 2016, we independently released a self-titled debut EP with four tracks, pressed onto 300 CDs. In 2019, we had 12 tracks ready that we wanted to release as an album, but once everything had been recorded in our home studio, the COVID crisis broke out… With the entire live sector shut down, we came up with a completely different strategy from quarantine: between June and September 2020, we released a new EP online on the 4th of every month. The first was the 2016 debut EP, which was remixed, remastered and released as “#1”. The next three were logically called “#2”, “#3” and “#4”. These were released online only, and each was accompanied by a video clip, in the hope of generating as much online attention as possible. Sven: We did not think the EP formula was such a bad idea, and when we had another eight  tracks ready in 2022, we released “#5” and “#6” online, one month apart. We did physically release both EPs on a vinyl album, with a “#5” side and a “#6” side. In the meantime, we have almost come to regard the idea of four-track EPs as self-evident, and so “#7” followed in March of this year. We are currently working on “#8”… Jeroen: It is not that we do not want to release an album, but our productivity is rather low, so it would take us two or three years to write and record enough material for one… For now, we are aiming for one EP a year (although we have to admit that even that is probably a little too ambitious for “#8”…), and that also keeps things a little exciting for us. Q: Speaking of those EPs, especially the latest “#7,” which took a while to arrive—by the way—to what extent is this new release different from, or innovative compared to, the previous ones? How did it come about? What were the different stages you went through, and what were the biggest challenges you had to overcome? Sven: The big difference between “#7” and its predecessors was that this latest EP was not recorded in our own home studio with Bart behind the controls. For this EP, we called on a good friend, Alessio Di Turi, who has a professional recording studio, and we spent three days there working on the recordings. By then, we knew what it was like to do everything ourselves, and we were particularly curious about the added value of a ‘real recording studio’, and we have to say that it pleasantly surprised us. Jeroen: Moreover, this way of working had the advantage of taking some of the pressure off Bart during the recording sessions, allowing him to concentrate fully on his musical contributions and leave the technical concerns to Alessio. Q: How does collaboration within Kregel work, and what creates the chemistry between you? By the way, what is your musical background? Bart: Our collaboration can be summed up briefly and concisely as ‘plug in and play’. We get together (almost) once a week at around 9 p.m. and play until about 11 p.m. After more than 15 years, we know each other inside out and know what to expect from one another. We create our songs together during these more or less weekly gatherings. Starting from a simple idea, we puzzle over the lyrics and music until that one magical moment when everything falls into place and we exchange a satisfied look of understanding: ‘OK, another song done!’ That process can go quickly, but sometimes it can be painfully slow: anywhere from a few rehearsals to ten or so. It has also happened that we spent five or six rehearsals tweaking a song before concluding at some point: ‘This isn’t going anywhere’… Without many words, we stop and move on to another idea… Different and better, no drama. Jeroen: We are not formally trained musicians and learned everything in the finest DIY Punk tradition. Bart has been the frontman of Vandal X and Flipo Mancini since his teens. I started a band when I was 16, in which I was the singer, but that role did not suit me. I stopped when I was 18 and bought a second-hand guitar. In the years that followed, I made a few half-hearted attempts to start new bands. It took many years before I happened to meet Sven and arranged to jam with him. That led to Feetfetish, and the rest is Kregel history. Sven: Before Feetfetish, I had never committed to a permanent band. I did have a guitar, which I learned to play without much of a plan, sometimes with friends, but it was only with Feetfetish that it became a regular thing. Jeroen: Those weekly rehearsals have by now become almost a physical necessity: putting the daily hassles aside and creating ‘Something Beautiful’ together with a few good friends — that is what it is all about for us! Sven: But there is also the romance of being ‘on the road’ together: the rituals of coffee breaks at motorway service stations, loading our gear, soundchecks, the concerts themselves, of course (and the kick they give!), packing everything up, and driving home at night… Bart: Not to forget the wonderful encounters! With organizers, promoters, venue volunteers, other bands, but above all with the audience, who are invariably enthusiastic. We seem to be part of a small but very welcoming scene of free-spirited people, connected by the magic of the underground. Q: You already mentioned it, but recently, you had the honor of opening for none other than P.I.L. here in Belgium. How was that experience, and what was the encounter like with the one and only Johnny ‘Rotten’ Lydon? Sven: Indeed, it was a great honor, even though we were filling in for the tour’s regular support act! We had been briefed beforehand that Mr. Lydon was rather ‘a man unto himself’ and did not like to be ‘bothered’ before or after a concert. Naturally, we respected that (the man had already been touring for months), and we were more than happy simply to be there at all and do our thing. Bart: Afterwards, we again received nothing but positive reactions to our gigs, along with excellent merch sales! Jeroen: Those two support slots were genuine milestones in Kregel’s existence! It was the first time we had played in such large, highly professional venues (Botanique in Brussels and TRIX in Antwerp), which were also almost sold out. What a luxury: perfect stage sound, and even a few stagehands at our disposal (as we discovered after we had already set up our gear…). All those circumstances, combined with the great reactions from the audience, made us feel as though we had risen above ourselves… Moreover, the very strong P.I.L. shows gave us, as ‘older youngsters’, hope for the future. Q: What else is written in the stars for Kregel? Sven: We have no idea. The only thing we do know is that we still get together every week with an enormous amount of pleasure, as we have been doing for more than 15 years, and that this has become an essential part of our existence. We hope that can continue for a long time, with the occasional concert (although we would like to play more shows than we actually do…), the release of new songs, and everything that comes with ‘being in a band together’, but above all the great pleasure we get from knowing that other people also enjoy what we do. Jeroen: After our two nights in the shadow of John Lydon, we agreed that we would at least keep going until we are 80… Bart: And now we can only hope that the stars won’t write a different story…

items.body: Alex Kourelis has been active as Digital Geist since 1999. The American artist has even collaborated with none other than Patrick Codenys of Front 242 on a joint album. Now, after a relatively quiet period, he returns with “Starcrashed”. This is a conceptual work—more specifically, an alternative Soundtrack that Alex K. composed for the 1979 film “Starcrash”. He analyzed the film scene by scene to create his own score, resulting in no fewer than 36 tracks and a total running time of around 90 minutes. From the very first notes, it is clear that this is a Soundtrack. However, anyone expecting conventional film music with orchestral arrangements and sweeping strings is in for a surprise. Digital Geist has always incorporated strong Electro influences, and this release is no exception. There is a generous dose of EBM, alongside Industrial elements, Acid sequences, nods to Techno, and even hints of Psy-Trance. Naturally, most of the tracks are extremely short. While this can sometimes be a little frustrating, it is inevitable given the concept behind the album. It is a shame, though, because the shorter tracks often contain some of the best material, with certain passages evoking the atmosphere of the Chemical Brothers or Praga Khan at their best. I was also particularly impressed by the superb mixing and powerful production, which sound truly ultra-professional. The only downside is that, although there are some longer pieces, I find these to be the least interesting tracks on the album. It is a unique concept—one could easily describe it as an EBM Soundtrack—and the kind of project that makes you wish more films or series would feature this style of music. Last but not least, the limited-edition USB release also includes the original film accompanied by this alternative Soundtrack. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Hard Time In Space”: https://digitalgeist.bandcamp.com/track/hard-time-in-space

items.body: These are liner notes by Stef Gijssels for two recent albums by Swedish saxophonist and composer Martin Küchen, first with Angles 4, second for his solo album. Angles 4 - (Relative Pitch, 2026) Listening to Angles 4 here and now, in 2026, feels like a warm homecoming. The album is filled with the grand themes that have resonated throughout the various ensembles over the years, from the Martin Küchen Trio and Angles 6 to Angles 9 and All Included . The quartet knows this material by heart, having performed these compositions for decades. I would almost call them their personal standards: they sound deeply familiar, yet they retain the same power and vigour as they must have had at their very first performances—perhaps now with even greater maturity, intensity and fierceness. The smaller quartet format gives the musicians more room to explore, express and expand, particularly across the relatively long tracks, most of which run for seven or eight minutes. There is a sense of space in the arrangements, but never a loss of urgency. The music digs deep into the history of jazz, drawing on the spirit of Mingus and Coltrane, while at times reaching even further back into the history of sound itself—and into the collective emotions of people living through dire times: war, oppression and other horrors. Here, music becomes both a source of comfort and a force of liberation. Whatever the size of the ensemble, this music remains as infectious as ever. Listen and download from Bandcamp Martin Küchen - Chase The Demons Out (Thanatosis, 2026) Brutal sounds. Heart-rending, bleak. Gut-wrenching and abrasive. Sorrowful, dark, mournful, ominous. One musician generating a torrent of expression through three instruments played at once: sopranino saxophone, two horizontal hand drums, along with cymbals, metal plates, and bowls. We know Martin Küchen from his work with the Angles ensemble—music that unfolds in epic arcs, sweeping themes that speak to a collective emotional space. This is the opposite. Here the music is stripped down to brutal poetry: visceral, concise, unadorned. Short, explosive statements. Limited means used to build intense dramatic pressure. Küchen’s anger at the state of the world is well known, and here it finds direct form in pounding drums and the wailing saxophone. Sound bursts collide and fracture, channeling raw fury. The opening track, “ Chase The Demons Out, ” reflects a world drifting toward totalitarianism. Its title echoes a phrase from 1970s Chinese state media calling to “sweep away all demons”—to eliminate those who think differently. The theme feels disturbingly current as war again ravages the Middle East, where rockets, aircraft, and attack drones serve the ambitions of those in power. The second piece, “ Mach kein Krach ” (“stop making noise”), recalls Küchen’s father telling him to quiet down as a child—something his son clearly had no intention of doing. The message is the opposite of silence: make your voice heard. Refuse passivity. Rebel, resist, speak up. Make noise. The third piece, “ Mit Ach und Krach, ” uses a German expression describing something achieved with great difficulty—through blood, sweat, and tears. Speaking out and resisting the present state of affairs demands exactly that kind of effort. Taken together, the three brief pieces form a suite: anger at the world, inner rebellion, and the search for the energy to act. Every saxophone cry, every drum strike carries elemental emotion—horror, pain, rejection, fear—pushed forward by outrage, anger, disgust, and indignation. These forces build toward movement: to resist, to act, to stand together. It will take effort. It will take blood, sweat, and tears. Once again, Küchen shows his artistic clarity. The music is raw, brutal, uncompromising—and authentic. The world needs this." Listen and download from Bandcamp Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: From solo piano to orchestra, the music in this genre bears witness to life’s atrocities; it reflects the change of seasons; it seeks to console and uplift. Our top pick reintroduces us to a fallen friend, but new composers make an impact as well; one can never tell where the next great album will come from. Soon the leaves will begin to fall again, and then the snow, and then the rain, and then it will be summer. These composers bring us through life’s transitions, always looking forward to the next, teaching us the wisdom of cycles through the beauty of notes. Our cover image is taken from Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador, covered below. Jóhann Jóhannsson has been gone nearly a decade now, and his absence is still felt. After a trickle of posthumous releases, we had grown resigned to the thought that we might never again hear new music from the composer. Meanwhile, Adam Wiltzie was working on unfinished pieces from a collaboration begun before the composer’s untimely death. We can think of no one better to tackle such a project. Adding to the sadness is the knowledge that Steve Albini helped with the production before he too was lost to the sands of time. Friendship Survival Guide is a tribute and a sonic keepsake; it’s a minor miracle that it exists at all. The first video is the beginning of a narrative thread; we can’t wait to see the rest! (Deutsche Grammophon, September 18). Also on Deutsche Grammophon, Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir reimagines her back catalogue with Robert Ames and the DSO Berlin. This Will Be Us breathes new life into these pieces and is preceded by non-album track “Floods” (October 23). The cover of Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador looks like Max from Where the Wild Things Are sleeping off his evening; but it may also be a young man dreaming of adventure. The album is an ode to childhood imagination, bolstered by copious choirs and swirling strings (Arts & Crafts, September 25). Third Coast Percussion returns with Vernacular, the percussion ensemble’s 25th album. Jlin is now a full performing member, as heard on the opening single Premonition (Rockwell, October 23). Klara Lewis‘ Opening is already out, one of autumn’s early highlights. The album is awash in shades of blue, from art to music. After the abraded loops of “Ta Min Hand “, the set moves from form to abstraction, shifting like light through falling leaves (Editions Mego, September 4).   Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen is a diverse set that addresses migration and memory through song, spoken word, voice and field recordings. The artist’s cello shines throughout the set, which culminates in a surprising rendition of “Shchedryk,” known to modern listeners as “Carol of the Bells” (Alumni Records Glasgow, September 4). Earlier this year, cellist Gaspar Claus impressed us with the score to French film Un Monde Violent. Now he returns with CELLS, which includes a contribution from Matt Elliott (Third Eye Foundation). The album is released September 25 on InFiné. Inspired by the work of visual artist James Turrell, Alyssa Weinberg‘s Pieces of Light, performed by cellist Gabriel Cabezas, plays with permutations of illumination. The album is preceded by the single ultraviolet (MASS MoCA, October 2).   Clerestory reflects its title, which refers to the windows in the upper section of walls, as found in churches. Jules Reidy uses this image to color the music, which highlights the interplay between shadow and light and whose single-track Side A is brought to light by JACK Quartet (Thrill Jockey, September 25). Twin Cities four-piece The Dust of Suns Ensemble offers Alyosha is a series of miniatures, inspired by Dostoyevsky, but with a playful aura. Released on September 1, early copies of the album are available on precious 10″ vinyl. We don’t receive many hurdy-gurdy albums, much less albums of hurdy-gurdy with violin and cello. Almost Starlight is one of these, recorded in a medieval church by Jem Finer (yes, that Jem Finer, from The Pogues!), John Matthias and Jay Auborn. The results are magical, mystical and ceremonial (Touch, September 4). Simon Goff‘s electronic chamber music is packed with violin and viola, with guest appearances by Anne Müller on cello. Interior Realms – vol. 1 is upbeat and life-affirming, on the surface a study of architecture but beneath this a treatise on the soul (Sonic Pieces, September 10). We can never tell where more eaze will head next, which is part of her appeal. On valley and structure, she heads for the heart of modern composition, even offering a score booklet. A host of guest starts decorates the set with new timbres and additional grace (Thrill Jockey, October 9).   Goldmund‘s In Each Moment is a gorgeous fall collection, inspired by the teachings of Buddhist nun Sister Dang Nghiem. The piano notes are as delicate as incense wafting to the sky, enhanced by some gentle ambient textures, producing a sense of perfect peace (Nettwerk, October 9). Chad Lawson‘s lowercase hush is as serene as can be, a prelude to winter. On held by evening, one can hear the almost hear the leaves as they start to fall (Decca, September 11). Jumping straight into that faraway season, Volodja Brodsky‘s piano-based Winterglare recalls the sun’s low angle in Estonia’s winter (We Are Busy Bodies, October 2). Piano player meets machine on The End is a Beginning, from the aptly named Postmodern Machine. The beats are warm and plentiful, but the ivories still hold court (Moderna, September 11). Some may recall that Björk’s first film role was in the feminist retelling of the Grimm tale The Juniper Tree. Forty years after it was written by Nietzchka Keene, the film receives a new score from Midori Hirano. The artist manages to tap into the tenderness and leans into the unsettling tension, with piano as the anchor and synthesizer as the encroachment (Viernulvier/Thrill Jockey, October 2). Ingfrid Breie Nyhus‘ Silkegul – Slåttepiano III is the third in a series of albums that investigate Norwegian folk traditions by means of the piano. As the nights grow longer, the notes will seem more and more fitting, like tales told around a fire (Lab, October 9).   Billed as a classical soul pianist, Alexis Ffrench releases the lush 24, two dozen pieces meant to comprise the soundtrack of a day. With tracks such as In Flight, crossover success is virtually guaranteed (Sony Classical, October 2). Pianist Sofi Paez releases Bodies of Water, inspired by Iceland’s diversity of natural beauty. Ocean is the first single (OPIA Community, September 25). Doubts and Loves Like a Mole is the new EP from pianist Nathan Schubert, preceded by the peaceful, brass-inflected single Schillerpromenade (Bigo & Twigeitti, October 2). Brandon Hopkins follows Three Commutes with Piano Etudes, Book I, six works of tender wisdom (September 25). On the cover of conditions for observing light, pianist Cephas Azariah seems to have been shot through with a sunbeam. The metaphor applies to the composer’s work, which also touches on ambient and electronic territory, while searching fro radiance in all of its forms (Anjunachill, September 3). With radiant contributions from Clarice Jensen and Spencer Zahn, Sova (Sophia Vastek) can do no wrong. As one might expect from the title, early single “Heavy Shit” is an exercise in darkness, but the album Alight! is a study of contrasts, anchored by Sova’s exquisite keys (Hout, September 4). Double bass and electronics merge on Fragments, an album long in the making; Fragment I debuted in 2025. By blending genres, ZKHR hopes to appeal to multiple audiences (September 19).   Dobrinka Tabakova has been accumulating the pieces of Stone Trail for nearly a quarter-century; now they are gathered in one place. The album is graced with numerous collaborators, and is one of our furthest-out releases, dropping November 13 on NMC. The first half of Episodic Memory includes a murder ballad, but the second is a vibrant instrumental suite that comments on the experience of trauma. Exceptet and Bendon Randall-Myers handle both with aplomb (cmntx, October 9). Daniella Ljungsberg splits Other Plans between vocal and instrumental pieces, but when she sings, she does so with reverence, honoring the Baroque nature of these tender Nordic folk tales (ORTHODOX, October 2). Alfredo Ovalles and Black Page Orchestra present The Art of Parties on September 18, preceded by the inviting single Dance! (PARMA). Richard Allen

items.body: Solythode maintains an unrelenting presence, often opening​ with uneasy ambient-noise structures before expanding toward the outer edges of mechanical rhythms and threaded bass lines that seem to operate just outside our galaxy. Industrial braindance and fractured electronic textures Solythode by Cathopsis   Their initial self-titled collaboration, tagged as “a seriously tough and targeted collection of harsher electronics” in 2023, seared through dense soundscapes. Their latest effort, titled Solythode—yet another spoonerism—sees both Cathode Ray Tube (CRT, aka Chang Terhune) and Solypsis (aka James Miller) working through ten tracks of industrial braindance and fractured electronic textures. A hardened The JD’s-styled synth-breakbeat pulse drives opener “Planet Downer,” while melodic blips and bleeps in “Plague Zone” push Cathopsis’ tone toward soundtrack-like passages and clustered crevasses, eventually locking into heavier techno-industrial thuds midway through. Dub-infested glitch elements cut through “Ghilie Suit Dub,” where broken beats form a dysfunctional whole, with an illbient power-noise sheen pushing the track forward into increasingly distorted territory. A serious powerhouse. Solythode maintains an unrelenting presence, often opening​ with uneasy ambient-noise structures before expanding toward the outer edges of mechanical rhythms and threaded bass lines that seem to operate just outside our galaxy. “Chrome Under Dark” stands out, its technoid undercurrent tempered just enough to keep ears and attention fixed on what might emerge next. Closing pieces, including the thudding ultra-bass march of “Chyron Prophet” and the crepuscular broken rhythm of “New Dreams,” make it clear that both Terhune and Miller are comfortable generating momentum from darkness. items.body: This is electro with its lineage intact and its eyes firmly ahead: studied, physical, detailed and properly funky. The lesson is simple. Know the form. Then push the production until the form starts pushing back. The roots of electro remain completely visible Interior Reset by Fleck E.S.C.   Committed electrologist Fleck E.S.C. brings his archetypal electro to legendary second-generation post-pioneer, pioneer ADJ’s Pyramid Transmissions for a full album workout as Interior Reset. What’s striking is how the roots of electro remain completely visible without ever collapsing into routine, lazy aesthetics or genre confirmation. These tracks are meticulously built, every texture and hi-hat seemingly calibrated to extract the maximum nuance from the intention. “Interior Reset” is the proof. Broken-tech funk, breakery and serious synthesis craft merge into something that feels both timestamped and timeless. It recalls the impact of seminal rarities that is the Scopex 12”s in the late ’90s (look ’em up), or later on Plaid with “Tether,” and the peerless LA Synthesis “Harmonic Disassembly:” the kind of electro you could play to an enquiring alien who asks, “So, what is electro?” Humanity would be doing itself a solid by choosing those and these. Rarified space devoid of cluttered copycat air. Elsewhere, “Technical Support” drips with grandeur and funk, groove-heavy and boldly beautiful, while “Cyclopedia” comes on like a link-friendly throwdown: body-popping, bone-shaking electro with enough technical muscle to make the point without ever showing off. This is production as practice, not display. Every move has purpose. Nothing is there simply because electro says it should be. “Opalissism” brings weight and width, its staccato arpeggios and spray-gun beats flickering across the stereo field, before “Interior Reset” opens the floor beneath the whole thing, using negative space and broken digi-breaks to let the darker pressure breathe. Then the full eight-minute version of the album’s primary cut arrives, beefed-up and beautifully unruly, all prime-time beats and synthetic muscle. “Moon Landing” follows with swell, swagger and synths jostling for dominance before the drums finally kick the door in. And then “Realisation Roads” takes the closing position and absolutely earns it. Fleck E.S.C., aka Franck Collin, goes hard and home, bringing the record down on a final surge of propulsion and precision. The album leaves the impression of an artist who knows the history intimately but has no interest in living inside it. This is electro with its lineage intact and its eyes firmly ahead: studied, physical, detailed and properly funky. The lesson is simple. Know the form. Then push the production until the form starts pushing back. Faultless electro. Not predictable but familiar enough to be easy to grasp. Interior Rest is genuinely stunning.
