items.body: Philippe Blache has constructed a detailed sonic environment where piano, electronics, repetition, and shifting textures create a sustained feeling of uncertainty, contemplation, and spectral loss. Liminal spaces, paramnesia, and the elusive nature of affective memory Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind by Philippe Blache   Philippe Blache‘s work has long occupied a fascinating space where neoclassical composition, dark electronics, and carefully sculpted atmosphere intersect. On Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind, his latest release for Bulgaria’s Mahorka label, those elements come together in a particularly compelling form. It is a dark and moody album, but there is considerably more happening beneath its somber surface. Blache has constructed a detailed sonic environment where piano, electronics, repetition, and shifting textures create a sustained feeling of uncertainty, contemplation, and spectral loss. The album’s conceptual foundation explores liminal spaces, paramnesia, and the elusive nature of affective memory. Those ideas are present in the music without requiring the listener to approach the album as a literal narrative. Instead, Blache translates them into sound. The pieces seem to occupy spaces that are recognizable but somehow altered, places where familiar structures have become unstable. There is a ​persistent sensation of movement without a clear destination, as though the music is wandering through an environment that exists just outside ordinary perception. Blache is perhaps best known as the mastermind behind the long-running neoclassical dark ambient project Day Before Us, and there is an obvious continuity between that work and this solo release. Yet Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind feels distinct in its approach. The piano is especially important, providing occasional points of definition within the more fluid electronic material. Rather than functioning simply as a melodic centerpiece, the piano often feels like another texture within the larger architecture. Its presence can suggest something intimate and human, while the surrounding electronics introduce ambiguity and distance. That contrast is one of the album’s greatest strengths. Blache understands how effectively a relatively simple acoustic sound can be transformed when placed inside an electronic environment. Piano tones linger within layers of sustained sound, while subtle shifts in timbre and density continually reshape the space around them. The result is music that can feel simultaneously close and remote. “Blache creates tension through accumulation and repetition. A tone may initially seem almost static, only to reveal small internal movements as the piece progresses. These details encourage attentive listening and give the album a considerable amount of depth.” ~Don Haugen The electronic textures are particularly impressive. There is a strong sense of patience in the way sounds are allowed to develop, overlap, and gradually change. Rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Blache creates tension through accumulation and repetition. A tone may initially seem almost static, only to reveal small internal movements as the piece progresses. These details encourage attentive listening and give the album a considerable amount of depth. There is also something wonderfully spectral about Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind. Its sounds frequently seem to exist between states, neither entirely present nor completely disappearing. This quality connects beautifully with the album’s exploration of liminal spaces and shifting memories. Blache creates the sensation of something that is almost remembered, something felt at the edges of consciousness but never completely recovered. The album’s melancholia is therefore not simply a matter of dark tones or minor-key piano. It is embedded in the structure of the compositions themselves. Repetition becomes important here, with recurring elements gradually taking on different emotional meanings as their surroundings change. A phrase or texture that initially feels stable can become unsettling when it returns in a slightly altered context. An intriguing and beautifully constructed work :: The collaboration with photographer and visual storyteller objet-fantôme, Angela Caro, also reinforces the album’s interest in unusual psychological and spatial environments. The music and visual concept share an appreciation for ambiguity, allowing the listener to inhabit an imagined territory rather than simply observe it from a distance. Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind is an intriguing and beautifully constructed work. Its darkness is balanced by subtle beauty, its electronic textures are remarkably detailed, and its use of piano gives the album a welcome emotional anchor. Most importantly, Blache understands the value of restraint. The music does not need to announce its intentions. It gradually reveals them. This is an album that rewards repeated listening, with new details emerging from its carefully layered surfaces. Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind is an atmospheric and thoughtfully realized excursion into uncertainty, melancholia, repetition, and the spaces between what we experience and what we can fully understand. Embodied Shadow Of Thy Secret Mind is available on Mahorka. items.body: DiN has built an extensive catalog through precisely these kinds of creative connections, and Juxtapositions stands as a particularly strong example of what can emerge when experienced artists remain genuinely open to one another. There is considerable craft here. Its sophistication lies in the natural way its many elements coexist and transform. The realization of a conversation that required time to develop Juxtapositions (DiN97) by Boddy | Scanner   Collaboration can be a particularly revealing form of musical exchange. When two artists with long-established identities enter the same creative space, the result can either reinforce familiar strengths or uncover previously unexplored territory. On Juxtapositions, Ian Boddy and Scanner, the recording identity of Robin Rimbaud, accomplish the latter with remarkable assurance. Both are legendary figures within the broad landscape of electronic music, yet they approach sound from distinctly different perspectives. That contrast becomes the central strength of this nine-track collaboration. Released on Boddy‘s long-running DiN imprint, Juxtapositions brings together two musicians whose individual careers have been defined by curiosity, exploration, and an ability to continually expand their respective vocabularies. Scanner has previously appeared on DiN through his solo releases An Ascent and The Homeland of Electricity, while his work alongside Boddy at Manchester’s Subliminal Impulse festival ​in 2022 offered an earlier indication of what their musical connection might produce. Four years later, Juxtapositions feels less like a casual meeting of established artists and more like the realization of a conversation that required time to develop.   Fragments, environmental recordings, and elusive electronic details :: The album’s title is particularly appropriate. Boddy and Rimbaud‘s approaches remain identifiable, but neither musician simply occupies a separate half of the sound field. Instead, their contrasting methods continually intersect and reshape one another. Cycling electronic patterns emerge and gradually lose their boundaries within more diffuse textures. Carefully articulated sequences create a sense of forward movement before dissolving into reverberant spaces filled with fragments, environmental recordings, and elusive electronic details. The opening “Exclusion Zone” immediately establishes this sense of unstable balance. Repetition and atmosphere coexist without either becoming dominant, creating a piece that seems simultaneously structured and unsettled. The duo understands the expressive potential of restraint. Ideas are allowed to develop gradually, and changes in texture or emphasis often arrive so naturally that the listener may only recognize the transformation after it has already occurred. “A Passing Trace” continues this approach with an appropriately elusive quality, while “Voltage in Bloom” introduces a more energized sense of motion. Throughout the album, Boddy‘s sensitivity to melodic and sequential development provides an important sense of internal architecture, while Scanner‘s interventions introduce ambiguity, disruption, and a fascination with the physical and accidental characteristics of sound. The combination is particularly effective because neither artist appears interested in forcing a stylistic compromise. “Sotto Voce” explores quieter territory, allowing subtle shifts in tone and atmosphere to carry much of the composition’s emotional weight. This is followed by “Intersignals,” where fragments of communication and electronic activity become part of the musical environment. Scanner‘s recognizable use of radio transmissions and found audio is particularly effective throughout Juxtapositions. These elements never feel like decorative references or conceptual interruptions. Instead, they introduce a human presence that is distant, fragmented, and often impossible to fully understand. Source material and electronic processing become increasingly difficult to locate :: That tension between familiarity and abstraction becomes increasingly important as the album progresses. Field recordings from old houses and reverberant cellars suggest physical spaces without reducing them to easily identifiable locations. They become acoustic environments within the compositions, their resonances and imperfections blending with synthesized sound until distinctions between source material and electronic processing become increasingly difficult to locate. “A Room of Hammers” is among the album’s most evocative titles and its slightly extended duration allows the duo to explore a particularly rich interplay between texture, resonance, and implied physicality. Sounds seem to occupy depth rather than simply appearing across the stereo field. There is a strong sense of entering spaces within the music, each one containing its own acoustic characteristics and hidden activity. The final third of the album demonstrates how successfully Boddy and Scanner have established a shared language. “Shared Frequencies” is perhaps the most fitting title in this respect, suggesting not merely collaboration but communication through common ground discovered in the process of making the music. “Mnemonic Patterns” returns to the album’s interest in repetition and evolving structures, while “A Fleeting Glimpse” brings Juxtapositions to a close without imposing a conventional sense of resolution. This album’s most compelling moments are often found in the details: a pattern that changes almost imperceptibly, a distant tone entering and disappearing, a reverberation suggesting an unexpected depth, or a texture gradually assuming a different character. Two distinctive musical voices discover new possibilities :: What makes Juxtapositions especially successful is that it avoids the temptation to present collaboration as a competition between recognizable styles. Boddy and Rimbaud bring their histories and individual sensibilities into the project, but the resulting music belongs to neither artist alone. Their differences become productive points of tension, generating compositions that move between hypnotic repetition, abstract sound design, emotional resonance, and carefully constructed electronic space. DiN has built an extensive catalog through precisely these kinds of creative connections, and Juxtapositions stands as a particularly strong example of what can emerge when experienced artists remain genuinely open to one another. There is considerable craft here. Its sophistication lies in the natural way its many elements coexist and transform. For listeners familiar with either artist, Juxtapositions offers the pleasure of hearing two distinctive musical voices discover new possibilities through their interaction. For those encountering their work for the first time, it is an absorbing entry point into the creative worlds of both Boddy and Scanner. More importantly, it stands on its own as a deeply considered and beautifully constructed electronic work, one whose subtle movement and hidden detail encourage repeated listening. Juxtapositions is an album about the productive possibilities of difference. Ian Boddy and Robin Rimbaud do not erase the distance between their individual sound worlds. They explore it. Within that space between their approaches, they have created something rich, patient, mysterious, and quietly compelling. Juxtapositions is available on DiN. items.body: Across Another World, Artificial Island keep things measured and textural, allowing minute sounds, gentle rhythms and shifting layers to carry much of the album’s character. A calm range of ambient-electronic soundscapes Another World by Artificial Island   London-based duo Artificial Island, lifelong friends Gareth Williams and Ian Prytherch, announce their debut album, Another World, bringing together some of their strongest material from previous releases alongside three new tracks: “Spirit,” “A Different Sun,” and “Departure.” It also includes their most widely recognized track, “Emerge,” a delicate blend of softened synth tones and lullaby-like melodies. All material has been remastered by Guy Davie at Electric Mastering in London, whose credits include Jon Hopkins, Marconi Union and Four Tet. Between cascading ambient-techno archways and ethereal waves of light, Another World generates carefully focused momentum. Traversing Another World, Artificial Island gradually unfolds a calm range of ambient-electronic soundscapes, with each track given room to develop through subtle shifts in texture and tone. “After Dark” is built around a floating atmosphere, soft electronic tones and light glitches that drift in and out of focus. “A Different Sun” introduces neo-classical elements, gently moving through cinematic textures and restrained melodic passages, while “Departure” focuses on microscopic details, weaving soft blips and bleeps aro​und low-flying beat pulses and a steady, understated rhythmic strain. As the album moves towards its closing tracks, “Lodestar” returns to spacious, celestial textures, balancing subtle movement with a sense of stillness. Closing piece “Lumen” takes a more distant approach, built from isolated ambient tones, soft electronic whirs and fragments that seem to hover just beyond reach. Across Another World, Artificial Island keep things measured and textural, allowing minute sounds, gentle rhythms and shifting layers to carry much of the album’s character. Built around atmospheric electronics, ambient textures and carefully layered detail, Another World should appeal to fans of Boards of Canada, Marconi Union and Carbon Based Lifeforms. The artwork was designed by Chris Bigg, who spent three decades at 4AD’s legendary v23 design studio alongside Vaughan Oliver, creating artwork for Pixies, Cocteau Twins, Dead Can Dance, The Breeders, and David Sylvian. Bigg has remained David Sylvian’s long-time design collaborator ever since. Another World is self-released on October 2, 2026, available across streaming platforms as well as CD and a limited-edition 2x180g white-vinyl pressing. items.body: The depth and breadth of Documents of Different Reality is truly amazing. Cold Blow have done their homework and their research. This is a compilation of archaeological detail that brings to life the momentous machine music of the 1990s. In Spara’s own words, the collection connects “dots that people might have not connected before.” Turning back the clock and digging into the crates to pay homage to the compilation Documents of Different Reality by Various   Back in the 1990s, the main means of communication for artists and labels happened in record stores. Afficionados and shop owners were the harbingers, acting as a go between for artists, labels and the audience. These gatekeepers would lead the bright eyed to the turntables and hand over a stack of vinyl. Coins jingled and sounds were exchanged. A keystone of finding new music was the compilation. Some imprints dedicated themselves to the format. Others used it to bridge geographical divides and knit together fellow analogue alchemists. Warp Records had Artificial Intelligence, Eevo Lute had Agenda, connections took hold. A glut of tapes filled bedrooms and car stereos as Detroit entered Berlin and Berlin arrived in Sheffield. Cold Blow are turning back the clock and digging into the crates to pay homage to the compilation and the artists who defined a sound and a time. The project is daring and I caught up with Pete Spara of Cold Blow to give some insights into Documents of Different Reality. For those who might not have come across Cold Blow, it’s a London/Helsinki based label with both founders hailing from Finland. Pete Spara, co-founder, describes Cold Blow as an imprint that aims to “release leftfield dance and electronic music often with a bit of a 90s vibe to it. Analog, quirky. Some new stuff, some anthologies, some re-issues, some compilations.” Documents of Different Reality is the boldest outing to date, a “labour of love” that started in 2019 when Halvtrak sent “a demo in 2019 with the title “Documents of Different Reality.”” The title “planted a seed for a compilation” that harked back to those early days of IDM. However, there was a sense that most “newly recorded music” didn’t fit that “very specific sound so the project ended up on the shelf for many years.” But, “the idea was so compelling” that is was “resurrected…as a retrospective.” Although Halvtrak’s “namesake track didn’t end up on the compilation” his contribution is acknowledged…in the liner notes, and he recorded the promo mix for Juno Daily when the release dropped. Technology and the passage of time permeate these Documents. When much of this music was released, there was an optimism of what machines would do for mankind and that we were collectively journeying to a better future. “I wanted people to think about the era when the music was recorded, and the present day, as two different realities. You can hear future-optimism in the music. What might those producers have imagined technology, artificial intelligence and everyday life would look like thirty years later, and how does that compare with the reality we inhabit now?” To connect the original period with a contemporary interpretation of it :: That hopefulness trills from the outset with a sublime example from the Netherlands. 2000 And One & Sandy Huner offer the spine-tingling “Eternal Life.” Nostalgic, yes, but also timeless, this is a beautiful example of ambient techno. Crystalline chords cascade, birdsong swoops above the understated double bass before a beat finally arrives to puncture the lush canopy. Humans are extended into machine in the refrain of “Life Forever” by Mind Control. A track conjured by Syzygy, Dominic Glenn, and Zendik, Justin MacKay, the Infinite Dreams mix first appeared on the UK’s Rumour Records in 1992. Lovingly restored, warm pads and strings are cooled by rasping rhythms as jazzy brass, echoing samples and twinkling notes orbit. The compilation’s focus is on the artists and labels of Europe. Originally, there was a plan to span the continents in search of tracks, but the scope of the project was already quite daunting. “It’s often difficult to reach the artists. There were tracks on the shortlist where even the original label had completely lost contact with the producer.” Searching the East, Cold Blow attempted to track down a “great Japanese track” and hit a dead end with all those involved being “totally disconnected.” Yet, this is part of the story and part of the compilation. The realities have shifted and some have chosen the “refreshing” route of not being absorbed into the sprawling communication networks we now find ourselves rooted in. Thankfully, there is an absolute treasure trove of tracks to choose from across Europe. LA Synthesis, superstars of noodling techno, have been drafted in for the blissfully bangin’ “Positive Negative.” A melody of stardust bends and shifts in a multitude of directions under the steady whomp of a kick. Iceland’s Thor pushes the tempo a little higher with “Break It.” Beat driven, this work melts minimal moments with electro grandeur as the sound of Detroit is reimagined. Methodical in structure, a slow and throbbing groove is peppered with sidesteps of elation. Unsung masters follow. Connective Zone released on A13 in the 1990s, alongside the likes of LA Synthesis and Stasis. More recently, the duo have returned with a number of self-released digital albums. “Electrons” surfaced in 2021 on their DAT Tapes collection. Recorded in 1993, the track is a soundtrack of a dawning future. Sci-fi streaked and immediately immersive, it is elegant and perfectly formed; a window into a seriously talented pair. “The optimism of the 1990s might have been eclipsed by something very different, but in these tracks there remains a poignancy and human touch that still hold the seed of what our reality can be.” ~Robbie Geoghegan Hidden amongst these gleaming gems of yesteryear is a contemporary addition. Barcelona based Permutation with “Atlas.” Spara remembers that “Dmitry & Edgar (Permutation) sent demos” when the compilation was being created. The “influence of the era” was immediate and their involvement allowed the collection “to connect the original period with a contemporary interpretation of it.” Reflective and ruminative, “Atlas” blends the aquatic elements of dub with the astral brightness that characterized the sounds showcased across Documents. Arguably, the most recognisable name on the sleeve is Steve Pickton under his Stasis moniker. Taken from the Inspiration album, which came out on Peacefrog in 1995, “World Out Of Time” is low-slung future funk. From the rattle and rumble of the intro, Pickton takes the listener up and away into a deep and soulful trip. Nothing is overly elaborate, the sparse elements and musicianship combining in harmony. A past name, one that is now gaining more attention, closes. Simon Walley released a burst of music in the mid to late 1990s before receding from the scene. Under his CiM alias he continues to delight audiences with his fragile style of electronics. The piece chosen is “Lead Point” which came out in 1998 on Headspace Recordings. Almost floating, this light and subtle work sails above ruffled rhythms and is a glimpse into the wonderful music of this musician. The depth and breadth of Documents of Different Reality is truly amazing. Cold Blow have done their homework and their research. This is a compilation of archaeological detail that brings to life the momentous machine music of the 1990s. In Spara’s own words, the collection connects “dots that people might have not connected before.” This “labour of love” is a testament to the artists and to Cold Blow. The optimism of the 1990s might have been eclipsed by something very different, but in these tracks there remains a poignancy and human touch that still hold the seed of what our reality can be. Documents of Different Reality is available on Cold Blow. Paul Banks built the song around indulgence undercut by consequence, pleasure and pain framed as two names for the same want, setting the scene early with the image “lick the sugar off the cane.” The London version stretches that tension out with the full band: Jack Martin and Adam Cullen‘s guitar and mandolin lines wind around each other, Maxime Arnold‘s harmonium deepens the drone underneath, and Dara Duffy and Jack Lawlor push the song harder on drums and bass than the EP cut allows. Banks has said the recording comes from “the last show on our debut headline tour,” and that the band wanted a version built around the full arrangement rather than the more minimal EP take. The band follow the release with a run of summer festival dates including Electric Picnic and Green Man, before returning to headline UK and Irish venues in October. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is an atmospheric quality to the guitar sound of Ian Alexander Griffiths, a guitarist born in Cologne, Germany, yet with one foot in America and the other in Europe, his musical interests shaped by his parents' dual heritage. He explores the English language, specifically how to communicate and convey feelings and ideas through it most effectively, using music as the vehicle. He is not alone in this endeavor; accompanied by keyboard, bass, and drums, the sound at times becomes cosmic, evoking a sci-fi epic. While there are echoes of Steven Wilson, his approach to the guitar draws comparisons to Steve Hackett, featuring a grand, expansive sound that isn't afraid to dip into hard rock influences or take a dark turn, as evidenced by the track "Exoplanet." The album is a cohesive whole, yet the first paradox, undoubtedly intentional, lies in the very concept of disconnection. Hints of a fusion style emerge in the guitar work, foreshadowing the solo career Alexander would eventually pursue.While more acoustic songs featuring impeccable technical execution, such as "Child of Our Times", may not stand out for their originality, it is in the more experimental instrumental tracks like "Five Bagger", where the guitar ventures into new territory, that Ter'Azur finds its strength. There are echoes of the Animals -era Pink Floyd, updated to transform that factory of analog smokestacks and floating pigs into a modern, digitized, and automated complex."Mass Hypnosis" is another highlight where the heavy guitar cuts through a wall of keyboards, breaking into a calm akin to blinding laser lights; the vocals are equally original, whispered, which makes them all the more menacing, while the quartet sounds incredibly tight. Once again, those solos that scale the crags, accompanied by the bass and carrying a touch of mystery in the notes, transport us to Spectral Mornings or Hackett's more recent material, until a heavy surge of keyboards dispels the mist."Beneath the Molten Sand," with its long, Arabic-inspired introduction, features a more settled vocal section that is better integrated musically. There are moments when the choir truly takes flight, with all four members singing, creating a genuinely oppressive atmosphere of tense anticipation that complements the composition."Nuke" stands out for the complexity of its arrangements within a layered rock sound, much like "Wayward Souls," which features a fusion style reminiscent of Pat Metheny during his own progressive phase. "Weather Report" is the album's title track and longest piece; while the vocal sections anchor it in a degree of predictability, the guitar work and instrumental rock passages elevate the song, offering surprises and introducing colors and textures that transcend a monochromatic blue.The album's title is highly revealing, referencing that transitional period when one drifts off, slipping into sleep while still awake. That transition shapes the album's trajectory, promising and accomplished, as it navigates the uncertain quest for a state beyond consciousness.

items.body: Fields of the Nephilim, the English gothic rock band from Stevenage, Hertfordshire, released “The Nephilim” on 5 September 1988 through Situation Two, an imprint of Beggars Banquet. The album turns 38 this year. It was the band’s second studio album, it followed “Dawnrazor” from 1987, and it entered the UK album chart at number 12. The record was made in a former courthouse. Sessions took place at The Justice Room in the Somerset countryside, a building where prisoners sentenced to death had been hanged on site. Bassist Tony Pettitt described the setting in a 2013 PopMatters retrospective on the album’s 25th year: “The place had a really cool vibe”. Mixing moved to Genetic Studios and the master was cut at Tape One. Sources differ on the production credit: the Situation Two sleeve lists Bill Buchanan as producer with the band credited in association, while Wikipedia gives the band itself. Brad Davis recorded the sessions, Timm Baldwin mixed, and Ian Gillespie handled pre-mastering. The line-up was Carl McCoy on vocals, Pettitt on bass, Peter Yates and Paul Wright on guitars, and Alexander “Nod” Wright on drums. ‘The Nephilim’ formats, tracklist and credits Situation Two issued the album in the UK as a gatefold LP with printed lyrics to “The Watchman” and “Last Exit for the Lost”, and on CD and cassette. Rebel Rec. handled the German pressing through SPV, and Beggars Banquet released it in the United States with RCA. The vinyl runs eight tracks: “Endemoniada”, “The Watchman”, “Phobia”, “Moonchild”, “Chord of Souls”, “Celebrate”, “Love Under Will” and “Last Exit for the Lost”. The CD adds a ninth, “Shiva”, which had been the B-side of the “Moonchild” single. Chris Bigg designed the sleeve, Simon Larbalestier shot the outer photography, Julian Calverley the inner gatefold, and Lynn S supplied the lyric calligraphy. “Moonchild” reached number 28 in the UK singles chart, well above the number 75 the band had managed a year earlier with “Blue Water”. Several titles point outward: “Moonchild” shares its name with a novel by Aleister Crowley, “Love Under Will” takes a phrase from his Book of the Law, and the lyrics to “The Watchman” and “Last Exit for the Lost” reference H. P. Lovecraft’s Cthulhu. The opening track, “Endemoniada”, carries a sample of Ron Perlman growling “Penitenziagite!” as the hunchback Salvatore in the 1986 film “The Name of the Rose”. Beggars Archive returned to the album on 20 October 2023 with a double-LP reissue pressed on golden brown vinyl and expanded with three bonus tracks. About Fields of the Nephilim Carl McCoy, Tony Pettitt, Paul Wright, Alexander “Nod” Wright and saxophonist Gary Wisker formed Fields of the Nephilim in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, in 1984. The name refers both to the biblical race of angel-human hybrids and to the magnetic fields around the Earth. Peter Yates joined on guitar in 1985, the year the band put out its debut 12″ EP “Burning the Fields” on its own Tower Release label. Jungle Records picked the record up and put the band back in the studio for the “Returning to Gehenna” EP. Situation Two signed them in 1986 and issued the singles “Power” and “Preacher Man”. The first album, “Dawnrazor”, topped the UK indie chart in 1987, and “Blue Water” became their first entry on the UK singles chart. “The Nephilim” followed in 1988. “Psychonaut” arrived in May 1989 and peaked at number 35, its ten-minute running time pointing toward the more layered approach of “Elizium” in 1990. For that album the band moved up to the Beggars Banquet imprint and worked with Andy Jackson, an engineer for Pink Floyd and David Gilmour, in place of Bill Buchanan. Its lead single “For Her Light” clipped the UK top 40 in its first week, and a remixed “Sumerland (Dreamed)” reached number 37 that November. The band played its last shows of that era in 1991, a two-day Festival of Fire at the Town & Country Club in London, documented on the live album “Earth Inferno” and the video “Visionary Heads”. McCoy left the same year. The remaining members recruited singer Andy Delaney and continued as Rubicon, releasing “What Starts, Ends” in 1992 and “Room 101” in 1995. McCoy started Nefilim, whose album “Zoon” was held back by label disagreements until 1996. McCoy and Pettitt announced a return at a press conference during the Zillo Festival in Germany on 15 August 1998. The single “One More Nightmare (Trees Come Down)” came out on Jungle Records in May 2000, reworking two songs from “Burning the Fields”, and the band played Woodstage, Eurorock, Roskilde and M’era Luna that summer. Jungle issued “Fallen” in 2002 with licensees including Metropolis Records and SPV; the band disowned it, and only one of its songs has been played live. McCoy’s fourth full-length under the Fields of the Nephilim name, “Mourning Sun”, appeared in 2005 with a cover of Zager and Evans’ “In the Year 2525” as a bonus track on the first 5,000 copies. A new line-up played the London Astoria in May 2007, the first Fields of the Nephilim show in seven years, and headlined M’era Luna in 2008 in front of a crowd of more than 23,000. Recordings from two Shepherd’s Bush Empire nights became “Ceromonies (Ad Mortem Ad Vitam)”, released on McCoy’s Sacred Symphony label on 16 April 2012. Beggars Archive collected the first three studio albums, “Earth Inferno” and a singles-and-remixes disc in a five-album box in November 2013. McCoy said in July 2014 that the band was back in the studio; “Earthbound” and “Prophecy” were played live that December, and “Prophecy” was issued as a single on 17 March 2016, produced, engineered and mixed by McCoy and mastered by Maor Appelbaum. Guitarist Tom Edwards, who played with the band between 2008 and 2016, died of heart failure in January 2017 while touring the United States with Adam Ant, reported at the time in Fields of the Nephilim / Adam Ant guitarist Tom Edwards dies aged 41. Beggars Archive has kept the back catalogue moving since then, with the expanded “The Nephilim” in October 2023, a 30th anniversary red vinyl “Elizium” on 5 April 2024, and a remastered “Dawnrazor” on 12 December 2025. The current line-up is McCoy on vocals, Pettitt on bass and Gavin King and Adam Leach on guitars. Thirty-eight years on, “The Nephilim” still sits at the centre of that catalogue, between the indie-chart-topping “Dawnrazor” and the wider reach of “Elizium”.

items.body: Skinny Puppy released their second studio album, “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse,” through Nettwerk on 5 September 1986. The Vancouver industrial band’s sophomore record turns 40 this year. It is the album that introduced keyboardist Dwayne Goettel to the lineup and pushed the group’s sound away from its early synth-pop leanings toward a heavier, sample-driven style. Dave Ogilvie and cEvin Key produced, engineered and mixed the album, which was released on vinyl and cassette through Nettwerk in Canada and the US and through Play It Again Sam in Europe; Capitol Records-EMI handled Canadian distribution, a deal that expanded the record’s retail reach from roughly 200 to 1,700 stores across the country. The cover, a photograph by frequent collaborator Steven R. Gilmore taken from a pornographic film he saw on a hotel television in New York City, later won Best Album Art at the 1987 CASBY Awards and landed the record on one of Tipper Gore’s Parents Music Resource Center lists. A 1988 CD reissue on Capitol Records added four bonus tracks, including the single “Chainsaw,” to the original nine-song lineup. The lead single, “Dig It,” received regular MTV airplay and a Billboard recommendation, and “Stairs and Flowers” followed as a second single; Skinny Puppy toured North America and Europe with Severed Heads to support the release. “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” streams on Bandcamp and is also available on Spotify. Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse by Skinny Puppy About Skinny Puppy Skinny Puppy started in Vancouver, Canada, in 1982 as a side project for drummer cEvin Key (born Kevin Crompton), who was also playing in the new wave band Images in Vogue. Key brought in vocalist Nivek Ogre (Kevin Ogilvie), and the two adopted stage names to tell the two Kevins apart. The pair self-released the “Back & Forth” EP in 1983 and signed to the Vancouver label Nettwerk that same year. A second EP, “Remission,” followed in December 1984, and the debut album, “Bites,” arrived in 1985 with Bill Leeb, performing as Wilhelm Schroeder, on bass synth and backing vocals. Leeb left in 1986 to start Front Line Assembly, and Key hired keyboardist Dwayne Goettel to replace him. Goettel, a classically trained pianist with a background in samplers and the Ensoniq Mirage, had met Key the year before, when his band Water opened for Skinny Puppy. He made his first appearance on record on “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse,” released 5 September 1986. Key later called Goettel “the master of sampling.” Skinny Puppy went on to release “Cleanse Fold and Manipulate” (1987), “VIVIsectVI” (1988), “Rabies” (1989, featuring Ministry’s Al Jourgensen), “Too Dark Park” (1990) and “Last Rights” (1992), their final album for Nettwerk. In 1993 the band signed to Rick Rubin’s American Recordings and moved to Los Angeles to record “The Process.” Ogre left the band in June 1995, and Goettel died two months later, on 23 August 1995, at the age of 31. Key and producer Dave “Rave” Ogilvie completed “The Process,” releasing it in 1996 in Goettel’s memory. Skinny Puppy reunited for a one-off show in Dresden, Germany, in 2000 and became a full-time act again in 2003 with producer Mark Walk, releasing “The Greater Wrong of the Right” (2004), “Mythmaker” (2007), “HanDover” (2011) and “Weapon” (2013). “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” turns 40 in 2026 as the first Skinny Puppy album to feature Goettel, who remained with the band until his death in 1995.

In recent years, much of their work has appeared on labels such as Zazen Sounds, Winter-Light, and, more recently, Cyclic Law. With this new release, Nam-Khar explores a concept centered on alchemy, specifically the transformation of the self; the connection to—and inspiration drawn from—psychoanalytic pioneers such as Freud and Jung is therefore evident. It is no coincidence that the album comprises seven tracks, a number of symbolic significance in alchemy. Here, Nam-Khar gives free rein to their creativity. While the music remains rooted in the Ritual genre, it is clearly much more than that. It incorporates strong Dark-Ambient elements alongside Industrial sounds and a pronounced Cinematic influence, manifesting itself primarily in deep, astral passages. Add a healthy dose of experimentation to the mix, and you get a sense of the highly diverse “Antimon”, where magical analogue sounds, acoustic instruments, and field recordings converge. The album oscillates between mysterious, dreamlike passages and others that are menacing and ominous. With “Antimon”, Nam-Khar once again delivers a compelling release that is sure to captivate a wider audience interested in the aforementioned genres. (Rating:8). items.body: Some artists move between genres as tourists, collecting a new set of surfaces with every release. Kontravoid moves differently. Across skeletal coldwave, heavy EBM, freestyle-informed electro, industrial club music, and dark pop, Cameron Findlay has maintained a character that can be recognized within seconds: disciplined drums, bass that seems to alter the air pressure, synthesizers suspended between metallic seduction and industrial alarm, and an abrasive baritone that sounds transmitted from a sealed room. That consistency amid constant movement has made Kontravoid one of the most important acts in the international darkwave and EBM scene. The Canadian-born, Los Angeles-based musician, drummer, and producer has announced a new full-length album, Sound of the Void, due October 2, 2026, through Toronto’s Artoffact Records. It will be his second album for Artoffact, coming more than two years after his previous release, Detachment, which came out on March 1, 2024. The announcement includes the new single “Without,” joining January’s “Mortal” as the second track available ahead of the album. The space between albums has hardly been empty. Findlay carried Detachment through Europe and North America, appearing at Wave-Gotik-Treffen and playing dates alongside Buzz Kull and Cold Cave. In December 2024, Losing Game Remixes returned to his collaboration with Nuovo Testamento vocalist Chelsey Crowley, while Crowley’s band Nuovo Testamento, Normal Bias, Auragraph, and Tassel each pulled the song into a different corner of the club. Findlay also continued his parallel life as a remixer, recasting Ekko the Strange’s “Reanimate,” Modern English’s “Not My Leader,” Mareux’s “The Perfect Girl,” Buzz Kull’s “In the Cut,” and Raudiver’s “No Sun Rising.” The list stretches from foundational British post-punk to contemporary dark pop, but each rework retains his familiar low-end physicality and severe rhythmic control. That versatility reaches back beyond the mask. Before launching Kontravoid in 2012, Findlay co-founded the Toronto synthpop group Parallels and played drums with Crystal Castles and TR/ST. Kontravoid gave those experiences a single, durable identity, allowing him to change tempo, density, and genre without losing the tension at the center of his music. Findlay’s forthcoming album, Sound of the Void, promises to seamlessly blend coldwave textures with thunderous EBM basslines and pulsating electro rhythms, elevating the body-focused electronic style that has characterized Kontravoid’s recent releases. Yet, “Without” hints that the album will transcend mere repetition of Detachment. The new single “Without” opens on a throbbing bass synthesizer, an alarm-like synthwave figure, and drums pressing forward in precise, heavy strokes. Findlay delivers clipped poetic lines through a harsh vocal treatment as warped synthesizers bend around him. When the verse breaks apart, his voice gives way to a flood of effects surrounding a series of shouts. Dark pads, driving electro rhythms, and lush basslines gather into a cold, nearly solid wall of sound, pulling the track toward something disembodied and otherworldly. The song sits outside any single darkwave, EBM, or coldwave designation, though every pressure point bears Kontravoid’s signature. It is a different kind of Kontravoid track, and a clear example of Findlay operating at the top of his game: widening the project’s vocabulary while keeping its identity intact. Listen to “Without” below and pre-order Sound of the Void here. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Sound of the Void was produced by Findlay and mixed and mastered by Ewan A. Kay. Dylan Frankland contributed live drums to “Without” and closing track “Phantom,” with Daryl Dee handling the live-drum engineering. Jean Lorenzo designed the cover, while Los Angeles photographer Corinne Schiavone, also known as Perpetual Mobile, supplied the original insert photograph. The ten-track album will be available digitally, on CD, and on clear vinyl. A limited black-vinyl test pressing with white labels is also available. The digital edition and CD arrive October 2, while the first vinyl pressing is expected to ship around November 20. Digital preorders include immediate downloads of “Without” and “Mortal.” The album received funding support from FACTOR, the Government of Canada, and Canadian private radio broadcasters. The run begins September 10 at Elysium in Austin and concludes October 24 at the SUBSTANCE festival in Los Angeles. The October 2 album release falls on the tour’s Kansas City stop. Spike Hellis and Normal Bias will join the bill in Spokane, Vancouver, Seattle, Portland, and Sacramento. Tickets and further information are available through Kontravoid’s official website. items.body: There’s nothing so startling as the appearance of a vintage concert tape, in this case some 47 years old, that might illumine your view of a musician’s oeuvre, even a slight shift in focus counting for much. Such is the case with the release of Cecil Taylor’s performance from a New Mexico concert in 1979. Part of the concert was lost, but on the evidence heard here, Taylor was at the helm of one of the finest groups he would ever lead, a relatively unusual quintet that consisted of alto saxophonist Jimmy Lyons (with Andrew Cyrille, one of Taylor’s greatest collaborators), drummer Jerome Cooper and two string players, the violinist Ramsay Ameen and Alan Silva, here playing cello as well as his usual bass. Among extant releases, the two-LP set bears some resemblance, at least in personnel, to It Is in the Brewing Luminous , recorded in 1980 at New York’s Fat Tuesday’s, which had the additional inclusion of drummer Sunny Murray in the band and Alan Silva playing bass, exclusively. His cello playing here is an essential element, especially for the way in which it combines with Ameen’s violin. In a sense, the Albuquerque quintet is a larger band than the New York sextet, in terms of what the opening up of the soundscape makes possible. Perhaps the most notable thing about the Albuquerque recording is the level of subtle and evolving detail achieved by the quintet and its capture in the extraordinary recording job done by Mike Wolff, who was regularly responsible for recording the New Mexico Symphony Orchestra. The University of New Mexico’s Steinway was also borrowed for the performance, giving Taylor a piano appropriate to his special energies. The unusual clarity with which Ameen is heard here gives the performance some of its special significance, particularly in the way that his contribution combines with Silva’s cello in a virtual string section. Jerome Cooper, too, is less polyrhythmic, less aggressive than his predecessor, Andrew Cyrille, who had been the perfect complement in the trio with Taylor and Lyons. What is highlighted here is the omni-directionality of Taylor’s music, from his thorough absorption of Western “classical” music as well as the jazz tradition and the general legacy of African music in America. Here those elements are present both individually and in Taylor’s special syntheses, those combined and foregrounded strings every bit as African as they are European. Side C is given over to one of Taylor’s trance rituals, a summoning of spirits -- equivalent perhaps to speaking in tongues -- inspired and unknowable language accompanied by incidental phrases from the instruments, random sounds and Taylor’s piano musings, now enacted directly on the instrument’s strings, all an essential component of the complexity and mystery of Taylor’s far-reaching art. The music that continues on side D is particularly spacious, opening up with Cooper’s spare percussion and the lyrical motifs of Ameen, Lyons and Taylor, evolving and flowering, still spacious yet dense with high speed content – some of Taylor’s most brilliant moments on record, the other instruments lifted skyward, until it concludes with Taylor’s gravelly equivalent of speaking in tongues, the very practice akin to the untranslatability of Taylor’s complex, contrapuntal, poly-vocal band music and the extrapolating lines and abstract organizing figures with which he guides the music from his piano keyboard. Live at the KiMo Theater is a special event, reasserting an especially creative and relatively neglected period in Taylor’s career. Live at the KiMo Theater will be released on October 16th, but you can listen to a track and pre-order now . Live at the KiMo Theater Albuquerque 1979 by Cecil Taylor Unit Email This BlogThis! items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”
